title: Debian votes to allow "responsible use of generative AI"
content:
Debian votes to allow "responsible use of generative AI"
	Debian neither endorses nor prohibits the use of generative AI
	tools in the development, maintenance, or documentation of
	software, packaging, documentation, and other media published
	within the Debian Project. We recognize that such tools can
	substantially improve the productivity of contributors when used
	responsibly, allowing volunteers to spend more of their limited
	time on work that requires technical expertise, judgment, review,
	and collaboration.
The Debian Project nevertheless expects that all contributions submitted to Debian, regardless of how and with which tools they were produced, satisfy the same standards of quality, correctness, maintainability, and legal compliance. The use of a generative AI tool does not diminish the contributor's responsibility for the work they submit. Contributors are expected to understand, review, test, and, where appropriate, modify AI-assisted output before incorporating it into Debian.

report.summary: Debian formally permits responsible use of generative AI in project contributions, maintaining quality standards and contributor accountability.
report.background: Debian, one of the largest and oldest free software distributions, has long operated through volunteer contributions and strict quality guidelines. As generative AI tools like ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot became widely adopted, developers began using them to write code, documentation, and packaging files. This sparked debates about authenticity, licensing, and quality control. Some projects outright banned AI-generated contributions, while others embraced them. Debian's decision comes after community discussion and a formal vote, establishing a middle-ground policy: AI tools are allowed but not endorsed. The resolution clarifies that the burden of review and legal compliance rests entirely on the contributor, ensuring that Debian's high standards remain unchanged regardless of how work is produced. This echoes wider industry conversations about AI accountability in open-source ecosystems.
key_points: Debian's policy neither endorses nor bans generative AI tools, leaving individual contributors to decide when to use them for code, documentation, and packaging work.
The project recognizes AI's potential to significantly boost volunteer productivity, freeing limited time for tasks requiring expertise, judgment, review, and collaboration.
All contributions, AI-assisted or not, must meet Debian's existing quality, correctness, maintainability, and legal compliance standards — there are no special exemptions.
Contributors remain fully responsible for AI-generated work, and must understand, review, test, and modify it before submission, preventing blind reliance on automated output.
The decision creates a pragmatic precedent for other open-source projects struggling to balance innovation with governance in the age of generative AI.
report.impact: Debian's stance gives developers clear guidance and legal safety: AI tools can be used without fear of project retaliation, but also without lowering accountability. This encourages experimentation while maintaining trust in the distribution's stability. For the broader AI industry, Debian's nuanced position could influence other Linux distributions and foundations to adopt similar 'responsible use' policies rather than outright bans. Regular users benefit because the review process remains rigorous, reducing risks of unverified AI-generated code entering critical systems. It also sets expectations that AI is a productivity aid, not a replacement for human expertise, a lesson applicable across all software development.
report.tools: Readers interested in Debian's AI policy can follow the project's debian-devel mailing list and the Debian Constitution. For practical experimentation, watch open-source AI code assistants like Continue.dev, Sourcegraph Cody, and the StarCoder2 models, which can be self-hosted. Debian's packaging tools such as debbuild and lintian remain essential for ensuring AI-assisted submissions meet project standards.
